summary: Explains the three client/server email models, offline, online and disconnected, and how IMAP4 can be used with each. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains three ways email clients can work with a server: offline, online and disconnected. It shows how IMAP4 can support each model and request only the message data a client needs.

questions: offline vs online vs disconnected email
what are the imap4 mail models
subtitle: Three client-server email models and how IMAP4 can support each one.

tldr.problem: Email clients can divide mailbox storage and processing between a client and server in different ways.
tldr.mechanism: The memo compares offline, online and disconnected use, and explains how IMAP4 can be configured for all three while sending message data on demand.
tldr.outcome: IMAP4 began as an online-model protocol but can also support the other two models without changing the protocol itself.

today: RFC 1733 is an Informational memo with no update or replacement listed in the unit metadata. It describes email models as presented in December 1994.

sections.title: Three Ways to Use Email
sections.content:
The memo defines three client-server email models: offline, online and disconnected. It says IMAP4 can be used with any of them, even though it began as a protocol for online use.

Each model trades off server connection time, server and client resources, access to multiple mailboxes and the ability to process mail while disconnected.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo describes three ways a mail program can work with a mail server. IMAP4 can be set up for any of them.

sections.title: Offline, Online and Disconnected Models
sections.content:
In the offline model, the client connects periodically, downloads all pending messages, removes them from the server, and handles them locally. The memo names POP-3 (RFC 1225) and UUCP as examples.

In the online model, the client works with mailbox data on the server and keeps the connection open. In the disconnected model, the client downloads some messages, works on them offline, and later uploads changes. The server remains the authoritative repository, and unique message identifiers help synchronize changes across clients. The memo names PCMAIL (RFC 1056) as an example.
sections.plainLanguage: Offline use downloads mail to one computer. Online use keeps mail on the server. Disconnected use lets someone work on downloaded mail and send changes back later.

sections.title: Request Only the Needed Data
sections.content:
IMAP4 sends message data on demand, so a client need not download a whole mailbox or the full text of every message. The server can process RFC 822 and MIME information so the client can decide which message or part to retrieve. The memo gives an example of downloading a 2000-byte text part while leaving a 40-megabyte video part on the server.

The client-server relationship lasts only for the TCP connection. When a client selects a mailbox, it learns the mailbox state from the server and requests more state information as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: IMAP4 lets a client ask for only the message or message part it needs. For example, a client can fetch a text part without fetching a much larger video part.

sections.title: Where Mail and Message State Live
sections.content:
The model determines where mailbox data lives. Message state, such as whether a message has been read or answered, can live somewhere else. In the online model, state can be stored with mailbox data or kept on the client or a third agent, using unique identifiers to connect it across sessions.

Keeping state separate can help when a server provides public data such as netnews and does not maintain state for each user. The memo says server and especially client configuration let IMAP4 support these arrangements without protocol or implementation changes. Its Security Considerations section does not discuss security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages and the notes about whether they were read do not have to be stored in the same place. IMAP4 can support different arrangements through configuration.

references.text: RFC 1225, cited as an example of the offline model.
RFC 1056, cited as an example of disconnected use.
